Ukraine: two hours with Putin at the Kremlin, then on to Dublin, as Trump's envoys want Europeans at the next table

On Thursday, November 12, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, envoys of Donald Trump, met Vladimir Putin for about two hours in Moscow, the day after the Abu Dhabi talks. No breakthrough, but Witkoff wants to bring the Europeans into the next round. The two men then rushed to Dublin to brief Volodymyr Zelensky [1][2].

The meeting at the Kremlin lasted about two hours. Apart from an agreement on a large prisoner exchange, it produced no breakthrough, according to the AP agency; an adviser to Putin called it “constructive” [1].

Vladimir Putin said he appreciated the envoys' assessment of the Abu Dhabi contacts and welcomed progress on the humanitarian front. He also warned that any foreign troops in Ukraine would be a “legitimate target” [1][4].

Steve Witkoff said he wants European countries to take part in the next round. Putin replied that Russia had “never” opposed dialogue with Europe [1][4]. In Abu Dhabi, the Europeans were on site but excluded from the three-way discussions, at Moscow's request [6].

Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Ireland on Thursday evening to brief Volodymyr Zelensky, who is attending the European Political Community summit in Dublin [1][2]. Zelensky says Europe will be at the table for the “next” negotiations [3].
The Ukrainian president welcomed the prisoner exchange, but repeated that Ukraine will not give up occupied territory in exchange for peace [6].
According to the Axios site, cited by Just Security, Washington has asked Moscow for a new proposal for a future security agreement between Europe and Russia [5].

On the ground, Russian drones hit Kyiv, killing a woman and injuring five people, according to the mayor [5]. CNN also reports that, according to Ukraine, access to Starshield, the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite network, is again restricted [2].
Key takeaway: Washington is now pushing to bring the Europeans into the negotiations, whereas Moscow had kept them out in Abu Dhabi [1][6].
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte remains cautious: he told AFP it was not yet clear whether these talks had brought peace closer [3].
Putin's remark about foreign troops sets a red line for the Europeans: he is willing to talk to them, but not to see their soldiers in Ukraine [1][4].
The core of the deadlock has not moved: Kyiv refuses to give up occupied territory; prisoner exchanges are moving forward, peace is not [1][6].

For you, peace in Ukraine affects energy prices and European defense budgets, and therefore taxes. If Europe joins the negotiations, France will have a say on security guarantees, and perhaps on sending troops.

Civil servants: unions meet Lecornu over pay, government rules out a general raise ahead of the November 17 strike

On Friday, November 13, Sébastien Lecornu receives the civil service unions at Matignon, which were absent from the November 9 social conference. They are demanding an end to the freeze on the point d'indice, the value that sets civil servants' pay. The government prefers targeted raises for about 900,000 staff, and six unions are already calling a strike on November 17 [1][2][3][4].

Public-sector representatives are received at 9:30 a.m. by the Prime Minister. The meeting was prepared by two rounds of meetings with the office of David Amiel, Minister for Public Action and Accounts [2].

Their priority: an “immediate” pay rise, by unfreezing the point d'indice and indexing it to inflation. They also want the jour de carence (the first unpaid day of sick leave) abolished and the pay scales overhauled [1].

Sophie Binet, head of the CGT, estimates that public employees have lost 20% of their purchasing power in ten years [1]. The CGT Fonction publique had spoken of a “missed opportunity” after the social conference from which public-sector unions were excluded [2].

The problem is getting worse with the 1.6% rise in the Smic (minimum wage) on December 1 [4]: according to the collective Le Sens du service public, 1.1 million employees, nearly 20% of the total, already have a base salary below the Smic and receive a bonus to make up the difference [1].

The government rules out a general raise and favors targeted upgrades for about 900,000 of the 5.5 million employees. The idea would be to raise the minimum index from December, without waiting for January 1 [3].
But since many of these employees already receive an allowance that tops up their pay to the Smic, the increase risks not being felt as a raise [3].
The union front is divided: the CGT, Solidaires, Unsa, FA-FP, CFE-CGC and FSU are calling a strike on November 17, while the CFDT and FO were waiting for Friday's meeting to decide [4].

Key takeaway: the pay of 5.5 million public employees is at stake [3], and each 1% rise in the point d'indice would cost about €2.4 billion a year, according to Bercy, at a time when the 2027 budget has still not been passed [1][6].

The point d'indice is the value used to calculate the base pay of all civil servants. At the “pay meeting” on July 8, 2026, David Amiel had already announced there would be no general increase, in either 2026 or 2027, in favor of points added at the bottom of the scales and more promotions [5].

This meeting serves as a catch-up: on November 9, Matignon had brought together unions and private-sector employers on the Smic, without the public-sector unions [2]. The CFDT and FO put off their decision on joining the November 17 strike until this meeting [4].

For you, if you work in the public sector (teacher, health worker, town hall employee), it's your pay that is at stake: without an unfreeze, it will stay stuck in 2027, unless you are at the bottom of the scale. If you are a user, expect disrupted schools, hospitals or services on November 17.

Veolia opens in Moselle the first French plant to extract lithium, cobalt and nickel from old batteries

On Thursday, November 12, Veolia inaugurated a plant near Amnéville, in Moselle, able to process about 7,000 tonnes a year of “black mass,” the powder extracted from used batteries. It is meant to supply strategic metals to European industry, and one day to battery factories [1][2][3].
It is the first French unit to recycle “black mass”: the powder obtained after shredding end-of-life lithium-ion batteries, rich in metals [2].

The process, developed by Veolia, is hydrometallurgical: the powder is dissolved in chemical solutions to separate and recover copper, nickel, lithium and cobalt [2]. The group says it recovers more than 90% of the cobalt, nickel and copper contained [3].
The black mass comes from Veolia's sites in France, the United Kingdom and Switzerland; a site in Slovenia is also planned [3].

The plant has been running since the start of the year, but it is still in a “qualification” phase (quality tests with customers) and not in full production, according to Jean-François Nogrette, Veolia's director of hazardous waste for France and Europe [2].
Veolia estimates that nearly 700,000 tonnes of batteries will reach recycling in Europe within five years, with more than a billion euros of strategic metals to recover [1].
Its chief executive, Estelle Brachlianoff, is calling for a “European preference” across the whole battery recycling chain [1].
The group has disclosed neither the amount of the investment nor its earnings forecasts for this site [1].
Key takeaway: recycling old batteries locally is a way for Europe to obtain strategic metals without opening a mine, and Veolia wants a “European preference” to protect this sector [1][4].
Lithium, cobalt and nickel are used to make electric car batteries; the Amnéville plant recovers them to resell first to European industry, then one day to battery factories [1][3].

But closing the loop remains a long road, AFP warns: to make batteries again, these metals must be turned into cathode precursors (“pCAM,” the base material of the positive electrode), and Europe lacks plants to do so [1].
The bet is on future volumes: with nearly 700,000 tonnes of batteries expected to be recycled in Europe within five years, Veolia wants to be ready before its competitors [1][4].

For you, the immediate impact is small. In time, a European recycling sector could make the price of batteries, and therefore of electric cars, less dependent on foreign suppliers, and gives a second life to the batteries you bring back.

Mexico: Trump threatens to double tariffs over a migrant caravan, Sheinbaum replies that none has reached the border

On Thursday, November 12, Donald Trump threatened to “IMMEDIATELY DOUBLE” tariffs on Mexican goods if Mexico does not stop a migrant caravan that set out from Chiapas, near Guatemala. President Claudia Sheinbaum says no caravan has reached the US border since Trump's return [1][3][4].
On Truth Social, Trump wrote: “MEXICO MUST STOP THEM, NOW, or else, tariffs on Mexico WILL IMMEDIATELY DOUBLE” [3]. He called the caravan an “invasion” [1].
The caravan, of about 1,500 people according to a Chiapas government source cited by Reuters, set out on Tuesday, November 10 from Tapachula, a city near the Guatemalan border [6][1].

At her morning press conference, Sheinbaum gave a different figure: the caravan numbered 500 to 600 people at the start, and fewer than 100 reportedly remain [3]. Another, coming from Honduras, should according to her be handled by that country [3].

The president says that “no caravan has arrived at the northern border” since Trump returned to power in early 2025 [4][1]. She rules out any crackdown or militarization to contain the migrants [3], speaks of humanitarian aid and wants to send them back to their countries of origin [1].
Trump did not say which tariffs would be doubled, or on what legal basis [1]. In February, the Supreme Court removed his ability to use emergency economic powers to tax imports [1].
What remains are the tariffs targeting Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles: those are the ones he could double, according to Mexico News Daily [2].
The threat comes in the middle of a trade negotiation: in July, Trump chose not to extend the free-trade agreement between the United States, Mexico and Canada (USMCA, or T-MEC in Spanish) [1][5].

Key takeaway: Trump is once again using tariffs as a weapon to obtain something other than trade, here a halt to migrants, while the two countries are negotiating the rules of their trade [1][5]. The targeted tariffs affect key sectors: steel, aluminum and automobiles [2].
In October, Sheinbaum said the two countries were close to a deal, but steel, aluminum and cars remained unresolved, and Washington had raised its demands from 54 to nearly 90 points [7].

The caravan's size is itself disputed: 1,500 people on one side, fewer than 100 on the other [6][3]. It was still in the state of Chiapas, on Mexico's southern border, when the threat was issued [2][6].
Sheinbaum is betting on calm: she refuses confrontation and points to the results achieved against border crossings, while continuing the free-trade negotiation [4][3][7].

For you, the direct impact is limited. But many cars and parts sold in the United States are assembled in Mexico, including by European groups. Doubling tariffs would raise their production costs and may weigh on their earnings.

Morocco: to curb soaring vegetable prices, the government freezes new exports of tomatoes, onions and potatoes

On Thursday, November 12, after the Government Council, head of government Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri announced the temporary suspension of new export authorizations for tomatoes, onions and potatoes. The aim: keep these vegetables on the Moroccan market and contain prices driven by food and fuel [1][2][4].

The measure affects only new export authorizations: the announcements give no end date [1][2][6]. The government says it wants to protect both the supply of the domestic market and the interests of farmers and Morocco's “African partners” [2].
An interministerial commission (bringing together several ministries) is now monitoring prices, with daily market surveillance ahead of Ramadan [4][5].
The same Council adopted a draft decree on direct social aid: the minimum flat-rate aid will rise from 500 to 600 dirhams on January 1, 2027, then increase to 1,000 dirhams in 2031 [3].
The exceptional support for road transport professionals, put in place in the face of rising fuel prices, is maintained [3][4].
The outlet Le Brief had already reported a suspension of sales of these vegetables to Africa “since last week,” which some exporters are complaining about [7].

The pressure comes from prices: in September, consumer prices rose 1% in one month, food 1.6% and vegetables 4.3%, according to the High Commission for Planning (HCP), Morocco's statistics institute [8]. Over one year, the increase was still 0.5% [8].

Key takeaway: Morocco is putting its domestic market ahead of its sales abroad, as the El Mansouri government, which has set the rules for its “first hundred days,” needs to show results on purchasing power [4][11].

The decision matters beyond the country: Morocco has overtaken Spain on the European tomato market for the second year in a row, with about 493,000 tonnes in 2025-2026 [9]. From January to May 2026, it supplied more than 70% of the tomatoes imported by Spain, about 46,430 tonnes [10].
Higher fuel prices also raise the cost of carrying farm products to markets: that is why aid to road hauliers is maintained alongside the export freeze [3][4].
The next test will be the October inflation figure, expected on November 20, which will show whether food price increases are accelerating [12].

For you, the immediate effect should be limited, since only new authorizations are frozen. But Morocco is a major supplier of winter tomatoes to Europe: if the suspension lasts, supply could shrink on European shelves this winter, with a risk of higher prices.

Myanmar: now president, Min Aung Hlaing remains banned from the ASEAN summit in Manila, while his army gains ground

The Philippines, host of the ASEAN summit (the association of Southeast Asian countries), has confirmed that Myanmar's junta leaders remain excluded from the bloc's 49th summit, November 15 to 17 in Manila. Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, president since April, will not sit there [1][2].

The Philippine Foreign Ministry announced it on Wednesday, November 11: the leaders of the Myanmar regime remain barred from the summit and high-level meetings in Manila [1]. Myanmar will be represented by the director general of the ASEAN department of its foreign ministry [1], Han Win Aung according to the outlet DVB [3].
Reason: the junta is not implementing the “five-point consensus,” the peace plan adopted by ASEAN after the 2021 coup [3].

His status as president changes nothing: Min Aung Hlaing took it in April, after elections dominated by the USDP, the army-backed party [2]. He had already been kept out of the ASEAN summit on May 8 in Cebu, in the Philippines, his first snub as president [1]. DVB describes this new exclusion as a setback for his diplomatic offensive [3].

Human Rights Watch wrote on November 11 to Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos asking him to keep junta representatives away and to increase pressure to end abuses [4][9]. Philippine opposition lawmakers also defended the exclusion, in the name of the bloc's credibility [5].

On the ground, the army is advancing: according to Myanmar Now, it has taken the “special military region” of the opposition government (NUG) and camps of its fighters, the PDF, with more than 1,200 soldiers [6]. One analyst estimates that if it reaches the Hpapun command, under blockade, it could control the border with Thailand [6].
Neighboring Thailand is worried: ahead of the summit, Bangkok asked Naypyidaw to prevent the conflict from spilling across the border [7].

Key takeaway: five years after the coup, ASEAN still refuses to treat Min Aung Hlaing as a legitimate leader, even after elections organized by the army. The junta therefore remains isolated just as the bloc hosts the major powers [1][2].

The Manila summit will be closely watched: according to the Philippine daily BusinessMirror, Donald Trump and 17 world leaders were due to attend [8]. Myanmar will be represented there by a mere official [1].
The junta nonetheless remains in a position of military strength: the offensive against the NUG shows the army retaking areas held by the resistance, notably near the Thai border [6].
For ASEAN, the stake is its credibility: applying its own rules to a member that does not respect the peace plan it signed [3][5].
For you, the direct impact is small. But the war in Myanmar already worries neighboring Thailand, and what is decided in Manila weighs on the stability of a region where Europe trades heavily.

Siemens jumps on the stock market with record orders of €34.8 billion in one quarter, driven by AI data centers

On Thursday, November 12, Siemens announced record quarterly orders, up 58%, and raised its medium-term growth targets. The stock gained as much as 4.7% in Frankfurt and helped the European Stoxx 600 index finish at a record, on the day Nvidia slumped [1][2][6].
In the fourth quarter of its fiscal year (July-September), orders reach a record €34.8 billion, up 58% [2][5].
Revenue rises 11%, to €23.7 billion, and profit from industrial businesses by 22%, to €3.9 billion [2].
Over the year, free cash flow (the money left after investments are paid) reaches a record €12.1 billion; the proposed dividend rises to €5.50 per share, from €5.35 [4].

For fiscal 2027, Siemens targets comparable sales growth of 9 to 11% and earnings per share of €10.20 to €10.80, excluding Siemens Healthineers [2][3]. In the medium term, the sales growth target goes from 6-9% to 7-11% a year [2][3].
CEO Roland Busch cites demand from data centers, automation and software, and says he is not worried about a slowdown in data center construction [1][2].

The stock gained 4.7% early in the session according to Reuters, and 3.3%, at €286.15, according to another reading [1][4]. The Stoxx 600 finished at a record 664.01 points, also lifted by Allianz and Munich Re, while Nvidia lost 7.4% in Frankfurt [6].
Key takeaway: on the very day the departure of Nvidia's boss was rattling AI stocks, a German industrial group showed that data center construction continues to fill order books [1][6].
Siemens does not make the chips: it sells the automation, electrical equipment and software that run these buildings and factories. Investors see it as a way to benefit from AI with less risk [1][3].
European stocks benefit from this profile: the CAC 40 also rose on Thursday, thanks to its low exposure to AI stocks [7].

For you, Siemens is one of the biggest companies in Germany's DAX index, present in many European funds and savings plans. Its record orders also mean work for its factories and subcontractors in Europe. No buy or sell advice here.

How it works: why an order book matters more than one quarter

An order is a customer committing to buy later: a train line, a factory automation system, the electrical equipment of a data center. It turns into revenue as deliveries are made, sometimes over several years [2]. When a quarter's orders (€34.8 billion) clearly exceed the same quarter's sales (€23.7 billion), the order book grows: the company already has part of its future growth “in the bag” [2]. That is why Siemens was able to raise its medium-term targets, and why the stock market reacted upward [1][3].

Gold falls nearly 3% and drops below $3,900 an ounce: with US rates above 5%, the safe-haven metal no longer pays enough

On Thursday, November 12, an ounce of gold lost about $110, to nearly $3,876, and silver fell below $50. The rebound in US rates and a dollar at its highest in 19 months drove buyers away. Gold has lost nearly 27% since its January record [1][2][5].
At the end of the session, spot gold was worth about $3,876.40 an ounce, down $110.60 (-2.77%) [1]. Another reading puts it at $3,866.51 (-3.05%), “clearly” below the $3,900 mark [2].
Silver fell below $50 an ounce, and the dollar reached its highest level in 19 months against major currencies [2].
The main cause: the yield on 10-year US debt jumped toward 5.12%, as investors reprice further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve (Fed) [1][3].
Markets now consider a hike in December certain, with about a 13% chance that it reaches half a point [4].
On January 28, 2026, gold hit a record of $5,311.31 an ounce according to Reuters, driven by the rush to safe havens [5]. At Thursday's price, it has lost about 27% since.
Key takeaway: gold suffers when rates rise. It pays neither interest nor dividends; when a risk-free US bond yields more than 5% a year, holding gold costs more in forgone income [3].
The dollar also plays a role: gold is priced in dollars, so a stronger dollar makes it more expensive for European, Indian or Chinese buyers, which curbs demand [1][2].
Paradox of the session: oil jumped more than 3% on Thursday on tensions in Hormuz, but fear of a tougher Fed weighed more heavily than the safe-haven reflex [4][9].

For you, if you bought gold (coins, bars or funds) at the January high, you are down about a quarter of your stake in dollars. For a buyer in euros, the loss is slightly cushioned by the rise of the dollar. Jewelry could also cost a little less. No buy or sell advice here.

How it works: why gold falls when rates rise

Gold is a safe-haven asset: people buy it to protect themselves from crises and inflation. But it earns nothing by itself. Investors therefore always compare gold with what they could earn elsewhere without risk, for example by lending to the US government [3]. When that yield climbs above 5%, giving up that interest to hold gold becomes costly, and some investors sell [1][3]. Rising rates also attract capital to the dollar, which goes up; and since gold is priced in dollars, it becomes more expensive for the rest of the world [2]. It is the same mechanism that sent gold plunging in the early 1980s [7][8].
Precedents: when gold falls from a height

Gold reaches about $850 an ounce, then Paul Volcker's Fed pushes short-term rates toward 20% to break inflation [7][8].
The metal begins a long decline and falls to $252 in August 1999, about 70% lower [8].
Gold loses more than 12% in two sessions, its worst two-day fall since February 1983 according to Reuters [6].

The campaign runs from November 12 to 26, and the elected officials will take office in May 2027 [6].
For you, the impact is small. Ecuador matters to Europe mainly through its exports of bananas, shrimp and oil.

news.2026-11-13-inde-inflation-octobre-6: India: inflation climbs to 6.09% in October and exceeds the central bank's ceiling, a first in two years

According to provisional figures published on Thursday, November 12 by the National Statistics Office, consumer prices rose 6.09% over one year in October, versus 5.54% in September. That is above 6%, the upper limit set by the Reserve Bank of India [1][2].
It is the highest level since October 2024, when inflation reached 6.21% [2][4].
Food is driving prices: +8.94% over one year, versus +7.74% the previous month. Onions cost 116.22% more than a year ago [2].
Rural areas suffer more: 6.63% inflation (versus 6.08% in September), against 5.41% in cities (4.88% in September) [2].
With more than 6%, inflation is leaving the central bank's comfort zone, which had not happened for two years [3][4].
Key takeaway: this figure strengthens the chances of a rise in the policy rate (the rate at which the central bank lends to banks) at its December meeting [2][3].
A hike would make loans more expensive for households and businesses in India, at the risk of slowing growth in order to calm prices.
For you, the impact is limited. But India weighs heavily in the trade of rice, spices and generic drugs: strong food inflation can push New Delhi to restrict some exports.
